name: Mustard bath

card.summary: A traditional warm soak with mustard added to the water, used for generations to warm and relax tired muscles and, by some, to promote a refreshed, clearer-looking complexion.
card.aka: mustard foot bath, mustard bath salts
card.note: Mustard left on skin too long or used too strong can inflame it.

quick.overview:
A mustard bath adds mustard powder or seed to hot bath water. It was standard home and medical practice until the early twentieth century and is still used in some alternative medicine. The appearance link is the claim that it relaxes muscles and warms the body, and historically it was also used for skin complaints such as acne.

Modern trial evidence for the bath itself has not been located; a 1996 UK patent describes mustard bath salts for easing stiff joints and fatigue.
quick.how: Mustard is mixed into a tub or basin of warm water and the person soaks, traditionally after cold exposure or exercise, or at the first signs of a cold. Commercial mustard bath salts are also sold.
quick.risks: Mustard applied incorrectly or left on too long can inflame skin. Historical quantities varied widely, and sensitive skin may react; crude mustard oil is banned for sale by the FDA and other countries because of its erucic acid content.

lead: A mustard bath is a traditional remedy in which mustard is added to bath water, thought to warm the body and draw out toxins [1]. It was ordinary medical practice until the early twentieth century and persists in some alternative medicine [1].

Historically it was used for tired or stressed muscles, colds and fevers, and even skin conditions from acne onward [1]. A 1996 patent describes bath salts with mustard and natural oils said to ease stiff joints and fatigue, especially after outdoor exercise [2].

chain: Hot mustard soak warms the body
Muscles relax and the person feels refreshed
angle.text: Users take mustard baths to warm up and loosen tired muscles, and traditional use extends to acne and skin cleansing. The appearance benefit is a claim of tradition rather than a measured outcome.

paras: Mustard has been used against inflammation since Ancient Greece, where Pythagoras is said to have recommended the seed for scorpion stings [1]. Mustard baths were applied to tired muscles, colds, fevers, seizures and many other conditions, and children were often given them for pneumonia or typhoid fever [1]. Warmth was believed to calm the body and slow a racing heart [1]. Some alternative practitioners today use them for chronic pain [1].
No studies found. Mustard seed contains minerals such as manganese, iron and magnesium that are described as anti-inflammatory, but no modern trial of the bath itself is cited [1].
Mustard applied incorrectly or left on too long can inflame the skin [1]. Historical sources disagree on quantity, from a few handfuls to a pound in a small tub [1].
